performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
question: How can a Sanctus be written almost entirely for quiet harp and strings?
intro: Where Verdi raises the Sanctus on huge forces, Fauré sets it for a harp, quiet string figures and a three-note vocal tune. Follow the one place where the orchestra briefly turns to fanfare.

sections.label: Dominus Deus Sabaoth
sections.mNote: the same pattern with wider vocal phrases

sections.label: Sanctus returns
sections.mNote: harp arpeggios and the violin melody return

cues.title: Harp, violas and organ
cues.text: A harp figure of rising semiquavers runs under two quiet viola lines, with the organ sustaining a chord beneath. The sopranos sing a simple three-note “Sanctus” and the men repeat it. Nothing here hurries.
cues.evidence: Pages 45–47 of the score give the harp figure, the two viola parts and the organ chord, then the soprano entry and the men’s answer; Wikipedia’s account of the movement describes the three-note soprano melody and its repetition by the men. The report’s level is steady at −16 to −19 dB from 0:10 to 0:50.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The full orchestra of 1900
cues.text: Fauré’s publisher Julien Hamelle proposed rescoring the Requiem for concert halls. The full-orchestra version was first played at the Trocadéro in Paris on 12 July 1900, during the Exposition Universelle, with Paul Taffanel conducting 250 performers.
cues.evidence: The Versions and History sections of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem give Hamelle’s suggestion, the date and place of the premiere, Taffanel as conductor and the 250 performers. The sleeve of this recording credits Éditions Hamelle, Paris.

cues.title: The same pattern, wider phrases
cues.text: Soon after a minute the soprano phrase stretches over a wider range, and the men’s answers follow. The harp keeps the same figure underneath, so the music grows through the voices alone.
cues.evidence: The report finds boundaries at 1:02 (0.87) and 1:14 (0.87), with level steady around −17 to −20 dB across both. Pages 48–51 of the score continue the harp and viola pattern under longer vocal phrases; Wikipedia’s description notes melodies increasing in range.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Angelic violins
cues.text: Fauré is reported to have remarked to the violinist Eugène Ysaÿe on the “angelic” violins of the Sanctus in the full-orchestral version. In this stretch a soft violin line floats above the harp.
cues.evidence: The Versions section of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem reports the remark to Ysaÿe, citing Jean-Michel Nectoux’s Fauré (1991). Pages 52–53 of the score show the divided violins above the harp figure; the report’s boundary at 1:14 supports a change of texture around the start of this stretch.

cues.title: The only fanfare
cues.text: The harp’s rocking figure gives way to firm major chords, and horns and trumpets sound a forte fanfare as the men sing “Hosanna in excelsis”. This is the movement’s only loud passage, strongest from about 1:55 to 2:15.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −16.4 dB at 1:50 to −7.3 dB at 1:55 and −3.6 dB at 2:05, with the report’s strongest boundary at 1:58 (1.00). Pages 55–57 of the score show block chords in harp and strings and three brass staves (horns and trumpets) marked f; Wikipedia’s description names the horn fanfare.

cues.title: The harp comes back
cues.text: The fanfare sinks to pianissimo and the brass then fall silent as the level subsides. The harp returns to its first arpeggios while a violin melody floats upward. The full choir sings “Sanctus” again, helped by the organ, with the altos finally joining.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −12.9 dB at 2:20 to −16.9 dB at 2:25 and −21.7 dB at 2:35, with a boundary at 2:22 (0.56). Pages 57–60 of the score show the horns and trumpets marked dim. and pp on pages 57–58, the harp figure and violin line returning on pages 58–59 and the choir’s closing “Sanctus”; Wikipedia’s description gives the repeated “Sanctus” with the organ and the altos.

cues.title: Who scored it?
cues.text: Hamelle published the full score in 1901 with a vocal score edited by Fauré’s pupil Jean Roger-Ducasse. Some critics suspect Roger-Ducasse of the orchestration; others doubt it, and the 1900 autograph does not survive.
cues.evidence: The Final version section of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem gives the 1901 publication, the vocal score by Roger-Ducasse, the critics’ speculation on both sides and the loss of the autograph.

transitions.title: The same pattern, wider phrases
transitions.how: Nothing in the accompaniment changes: the harp keeps its rising semiquavers and the violas their quiet figures. The change is in the voices. After the three-note “Sanctus”, the sopranos’ phrase at letter B stretches over a wider range to “Dominus Deus Sabaoth”, and the men’s answers follow. Fauré lets the vocal line grow while the accompaniment stays still, so the music intensifies without any change of pace.
transitions.evidence: The report finds boundaries at 1:02 (0.87) and 1:14 (0.87), with level steady between −17 and −20 dB. Pages 49–51 of the score show the unchanged harp and viola pattern beneath the longer vocal phrases; the timing describes the whole join.

transitions.title: The men fall silent; sopranos continue
transitions.how: At letter C the men’s voices stop and the sopranos carry “Pleni sunt coeli et terra” (“heaven and earth are full”) alone, marked “sempre dolce”; the men answer “gloria tua” a page later. The harp continues its figure, and the violins, divided, add a line above it while the cellos continue with a sustained note marked “arco”. The texture thins to one vocal line over the accompaniment, a contrast with the exchange of voices that opened the movement.
transitions.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 1:14 (0.87) with only a small level change (−16.9 dB at 1:15, −18.8 dB at 1:20). Page 52 of the score (letter C) gives the soprano line marked sempre dolce, the divided violins and the cello note marked arco; page 53 gives the men’s “gloria tua”.

transitions.title: A hush becomes a fanfare
transitions.how: The men’s “gloria tua” closes softly, and “Hosanna in excelsis” begins at letter D, also softly, in the sopranos. Then the music builds: the harp’s arpeggios turn into firm chords, the strings follow with block chords, and horns and trumpets answer with a fanfare marked forte. The men declare “Hosanna”, and the sopranos answer in diminuendo. Fauré changes the orchestra’s tone from dreamy to firm for a single outburst, then withdraws it.
transitions.evidence: The report finds boundaries at 1:40 (0.94), 1:52 (0.81) and 1:58 (1.00), with level rising from −16.4 dB at 1:50 to −7.3 dB at 1:55 and −3.6 dB at 2:05. Pages 54–56 of the score (letters D and F) show the build to block chords and the horn and trumpet staves marked f.

transitions.title: The fanfare sinks; the harp returns
transitions.how: The fanfare dies away as the sopranos answer “Hosanna” in diminuendo. The horns and trumpets sink to pianissimo and fall silent by the next page, the harp returns to its opening arpeggios, and a violin melody floats upward over them. The full choir then sings “Sanctus” again, helped by the organ, with the altos finally joining. The movement ends as it began, with harp and strings, and with the fanfare withdrawn.
transitions.evidence: Relative level falls from −12.9 dB at 2:20 to −16.9 dB at 2:25 and −21.7 dB at 2:35, with a boundary at 2:22 (0.56). Pages 57–60 of the score show the brass staves emptying, the harp arpeggios returning and the choir’s closing “Sanctus”.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: III. Sanctus, printed pp. 45–60. The flute, clarinet, bassoon, trombone and timpani staves are empty; the double bass part is not tracked. Entries are set from the page layout and the report’s boundaries, so an instrument that plays in only part of a span is listed for the whole span.

timeline.note: Harp arpeggios and two viola lines over a sustained organ chord.
The sopranos sing the three-note Sanctus; the men repeat it, with the cellos sounding under their answer.
The violins enter pianissimo above the harp and violas.
The sopranos sing Pleni sunt coeli over harp and divided violins with sustained cellos; the men answer a page later.
Horns and trumpets sound a forte fanfare over block chords as the men sing Hosanna.
The fanfare sinks to pianissimo as the sopranos answer Hosanna; the harp arpeggios begin to return.
The brass are silent; a violin melody floats upward over the harp arpeggios.
The choir repeats Sanctus with the organ and the altos; harp and strings sustain to the final chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; neither has a solo part in this movement. The organist is named on the sleeve (“Chanoine Henri Carol”), not on Commons.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.
alts: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.51 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 1, track 3 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+60 cents (CQT histogram) and −0.38 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning); the report’s pitch-class labels read E♭ major as E major, which places the offset on the sharp side); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: A church organist who made the French song and the chamber ensemble laboratories for harmony.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; piano with Camille Saint-Saëns
Madeleine: choirmaster 1877–96, organist 1896–1905 · Paris Conservatoire: composition professor 1896–1905, director 1905–20
Mélodies, piano music, chamber music, Requiem, the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
Fauré learned his trade in a school for church musicians. His father was a schoolmaster in the Ariège; at nine, Gabriel was sent to Louis Niedermeyer’s recently founded school in Paris, where plainchant, Renaissance polyphony, organ playing and counterpoint belonged to the ordinary curriculum. The education matters to the harmony. A melody can cadence in minor with an unsharpened seventh degree; a chord can emerge from the independent movement of voices. These possibilities were practical knowledge before they became a recognisable Fauré style.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class and introduced the pupils to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Teacher and pupil remained friends for more than sixty years. Fauré’s graduation work, the Cantique de Jean Racine of 1865, already joins the two educations: a flowing keyboard accompaniment beneath a choral texture whose entries are controlled by contrapuntal discipline. Its French text is Racine’s paraphrase of a Latin hymn. The bass supports long phrases that carry the upper voices across the bar-lines.
